                                  PREFACE
        It has taken years of efforts in compiling, checking and re-checking
   of our material before these are printed and came in the hands of
   readers. My colleagues and I have. spent quite a few years going around
   the district and collecting informations. I hope this comes upto the
   expe9tations 0.£ readers as a sing\e best source of information on the
   Mahasu District.
        Considerable material has been \ collected over several years to make
. this a comprehensive reference book. In the words of Ibbetson in his pre-
 \ face to his very famous Punjab Census Report of 1881 "A Census Repor,t
   ~s not meant merely for the informatiJon of the Secretariat; it is intended
   to be constantly referred to in every office of the Province. The mere
   re~ults would ill serve this end in the absense of an interpreter. It is of
   bu't small advantage to cast voluminous tables oj naked figures at the
heads of District Officers, without at the same time explaining what they
rep'):esent, which can be do~e by no one. but him who compiled them, and
drawing from 'them the more important conclusion$, to which they lead,
which few w~U draw but he whose special business it is to do so". This
 comp,reliensiv,e reference book has to be a handy reference book for the
 Administrato;rs, Planners and Scholarp. It is not meant to be taken up for
'leisurely reading but to obtain some specific information. Therefore, it is
 very neces~~l'Y that this should be complete, should be brief and should
 be very relevant and precise. We have collected material from many
 sourc~s- a~d many old records had to be consul ted and then checked and
 re-checkeri oyer long period.
        It is the, keenness of Shri Asok Mitra, rcs, Registrar General, India
 to have guided us in' this work. His devotion to the Census Organisation
 is only ma,tched. by his versatility and many of Us have only achieved a
 certairr' degree of completeness in our work because of his interest and
 guidance.!
        Different parts of the volume present the vil.lage-wise statistics and
 brief write-ups on Education, Industry, Health, Community Development,
 Animal Husbandry and Co-operation. Apart from certain data, most of
 the other data, particularly regarding village directory is collected by us
 from r961 Census Schedules. I have heavily leaned on old records, files,
  notes and reference books and have also toured this Pradesh fairly
  extensively year-after-year. Mahasu is the District which has undergone
 some very obvious changes. There are some good roads, hospitals.
 educational facilities, agr.icultural practices have all given this District
  surprises which many people had never anticipated. The interior and in-
  accessible areas continue to receive due attention.
        In this book I have been assisted by devoted and hard working
  colleagues. They have burnt their mid-night oil and have toiled on their
  holidays apart of being to difficult areas over the Pradesh. And with the
  kjnd help that I have received from the Government of India Press,
  Simla, it gives me a great pleasure and silent p.ride to see this report
  cQmpleted: This report should have been printed much earlier but for a
  number of reasons beyond control.            -
         Right from the highest to the humblest my colleagues and I have
  received appreciable considerations. With well over nearly 50 publica-
  tions in hand, readers would realise that it was a pretty. arduous and at.
  ti:q:les seemed' back breaking. This was an opportunity once in our life
  time and we were obsessed to produce something of enduring vaJue. I do
  ~ot know_ how far we have succeeded and leave this to my readers to
  Judge. I hope my readers would find this of interest.
                                              RAM CHANDRA PAL SINGH
  Boswell:
  Simla-5.

   The household furniturfe consists of cots
and mats of rice stalks or date palms. Two
or three wooden boxes or steel trunks are
kept and used for keeping valuables and
clothes. Very few in the rural areas keep
chairs, tables or modern items of furniture.
Utensils are of brass, bronze and aluminium.
Radio sets, sewing machines, oil stoves and
similar items are steadi'ly finding their way
into well-to-do families. Many villages have
been electrified. Table lamps and electric
irons are found here and there.
